Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corporation Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corporation's Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; David Patel, Chief Financial Officer; and Maria Gonzalez, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Sarah Thompson.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corporation delivered solid results in Q2, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust production growth and meaningful efficiency gains across our portfolio. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on advancing future development plans and unlocking substantial resource potential that positions us for multi-year growth. We are focused on executing our low-cost operator strategy amid WTI prices around $78 per barrel and Henry Hub gas at $2.85 per MMBtu. Finally, we are taking steps to maintain capital discipline while returning significant value to shareholders.

I'm pleased to dive into our forward-looking development strategy and the substantial resource upside that positions Apex for multi-year growth in this dynamic Oil & Gas landscape. As you know, we've delivered another quarter of strong execution under these conditions that underscore our low-cost, high-margin inventory.

Let me start with the big picture: our five-year development plan through 2029 calls for $12-15 billion in total capital expenditures, with 70% allocated to drilling and completions in our core U.S. onshore assets. This disciplined approach targets a production ramp from our current 250,000 Boe/d to 400,000 Boe/d by year-end 2027, implying a 15% CAGR. We're funding this entirely from free cash flow at current strip prices, maintaining our net debt to EBITDAX ratio below 0.8x and returning 50-60% of FCF to shareholders via buybacks and our progressive dividend, now yielding 2.2%.

Turning to resource potential, our year-end 2023 reserves—audited by Netherland, Sewell & Associates—stood at 1.2 billion Boe proved, 2.1 billion Boe proved plus probable, and 3.4 billion Boe proved plus probable plus possible. This equates to a robust reserves-to-production ratio of 13 years at proved, extending to over 30 years at the 3P level. We've grown proved plus probable reserves by 18% year-over-year through the drillbit, achieving a reserves replacement ratio of 220% in the first nine months—well above our 120-150% long-term target. Contingent resources, unrisked, add another 1.5 billion Boe, primarily in emerging acreage.

Let's drill down regionally, starting with the Permian Basin, which accounts for 65% of our production and 55% of our D&C capex. Our 450,000 net acres in the Delaware and Midland sub-basins are among the industry's best, with average breakevens of $35-40 WTI. In 2025, we'll deploy 25 operated rigs and 8 frac crews, targeting 350 gross wells. We've extended lateral lengths to 12,000-15,000 feet in our Wolfcamp A and B benches, boosting estimated ultimate recoveries to 1.8-2.2 Mboe per well—a 25% uplift from 2023 vintages, driven by our proprietary ApexFlow completion design. This includes 3,000 lbs/ft proppant intensity, 60 bpm pump rates, and diverter tech, achieving 30-day IPs averaging 1,800 Boe/d, 75% oil, across our last 50 wells.

Resource-wise, we've certified 850 MMboe proved plus probable in the Permian, with 400 MMboe of low-risk inventory ready to drill at sub-$40 breakevens. We're also piloting CO2-EOR in our legacy waterflood units, injecting 500 MMcfd sourced from our own emissions, targeting a 15-20% recovery factor uplift. This aligns with our net-zero Scope 1+2 ambitions by 2035, with current carbon intensity at 4.2 kg CO2e/Boe—20% below peer average.

Moving to the Eagle Ford, our 180,000 net acres in Karnes and DeWitt counties deliver 55% oil cuts and some of the lowest gas breakevens in the play at $1.80/MMBtu. Here, 2025 capex is $800 million for 120 wells, focusing on our Pearsall Shale upside. Recent 10,000-ft laterals have posted 45-day IPs of 1,400 Boe/d, with EURs of 1.2 MMboe. We've added 250 MMboe to proved plus probable reserves via appraisal, and our seismic reprocessing—using full waveform inversion—has illuminated 300 drilling locations in the deeper Austin Chalk, where initial tests show 20% porosity and TOC over 4%.

In the Haynesville Shale, gas-focused with 120,000 net acres in northwest Louisiana, we're ramping to 80 wells in 2025 amid LNG export demand from Plaquemines and Golden Pass projects coming online. Our HyperFrac design—2,500-foot stages, 40 bpm rates—has unlocked 25 Bcf EURs per well, with 60-day IPs exceeding 15 MMcf/d. This positions us to capture $3.50+ Henry Hub pricing as U.S. exports hit 14 Bcf/d in 2025. Reserves here grew 12% to 450 Bcf proved plus probable, with a bolt-on acquisition pending close adding 100 Bcf at $0.15/Mcfe.

Offshore, our Gulf of Mexico portfolio shines with a 25% working interest in the $2.5 billion Winterfell project, partnered with Beacon Offshore. First oil is on track for Q4 2025 at 50,000 Boe/d gross, with our net share ramping to 12,500 Boe/d. We've booked 120 MMboe proved plus probable, with total resource potential exceeding 300 MMboe unrisked. Subsalt imaging via our joint-industry reverse time migration has de-risked two follow-on sidetracks. Longer-term, we're evaluating tie-backs to our Lobster field, leveraging existing FPSO infrastructure to keep development costs under $25/Boe.

Internationally, our 15% stake in the Stabroek Block offshore Guyana holds 200 MMboe net proved plus probable contingent resources. With Yellowtail FPSO spudding this quarter, we anticipate development sanction in 2026, targeting 40,000 Boe/d gross plateau. Guyana's 20+ billion barrel potential remains a high-impact lever, with breakevens below $30 amid fiscal stability.

Technologically, we're leaning into digital transformation: our ReservoirAI platform, powered by machine learning from Chevron-partnered datasets, optimizes frac staging in real-time, reducing water use by 15% and boosting NPV10 by 20%. We've deployed fiber-optic DTS/DAS for real-time diagnostics, cutting parent-child interference by 30% in the Permian.

Strategically, this plan hedges against volatility: 60% of 2025 capex is unhedged to capture upside, but we've locked 50% of oil at $75 via collars. Amid energy transition, we're allocating 10% of capex to CCUS and electrification—partnering with Occidental on Direct Air Capture hubs—and growing our LNG marketing book to 200 TBtu/year.

Risks include service inflation at 5-7% YoY, but our term contracts with Halliburton and Patterson-UTI cap exposure. Regulatory headwinds like Delaware Basin curtailments are manageable via our produced water recycling at 95% rates.

In summary, our 5+ years of Tier 1 inventory, technical edge, and capital discipline deliver 15-20% IRR projects at $70 WTI. We're not chasing barrels; we're compounding value.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Patel to discuss our financial results in more detail.

David Patel: Thank you, Sarah. As Sarah mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.8 billion, up 22% year-over-year. Operating income was $950 million, and net income was $720 million. We generated $850 million in free cash flow and returned $500 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $5.2 billion in debt and $2.1 billion in cash.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining Apex Energy Corp's Q2 2024 earnings call. Today, I'd like to dive deep into one of our key operational efficiency metrics: operating expenses per barrel of oil equivalent, or OpEx per BOE. This is a cornerstone of our value creation in the Oil & Gas sector, especially as we navigate a volatile WTI crude environment averaging $78 per barrel in Q2, down from $82 in Q1 amid softening global demand from China's economic slowdown and building OPEC+ inventories.

For context, our OpEx per BOE encompasses lease operating expenses, gathering and transportation costs, workover and maintenance CapEx, and production taxes—excluding non-cash DD&A and G&A. Let's start with the trend analysis, which underscores our relentless focus on cost discipline.

Over the past five years, we've driven OpEx per BOE down by 28% from $11.85 in FY2019 to $8.52 in FY2023, and further to an all-time low of $7.98 in Q2 2024—a sequential 4% improvement from $8.32 in Q1 and 12% YoY from $9.06. This trajectory mirrors industry leaders like Pioneer Natural Resources and ExxonMobil's Permian assets, but we've outperformed the peer average of $9.50 per BOE as reported in the latest Dallas Fed Energy Survey.

Breaking it down by basin: In FY2019, Permian was $9.45, Eagle Ford $12.20, Bakken $14.80, Gulf of Mexico $18.50, and company total $11.85. By FY2022, those figures improved to Permian $8.20, Eagle Ford $9.85, Bakken $11.20, GoM $15.40, total $9.75. In Q2 2023, Permian $7.90, Eagle Ford $9.40, Bakken $10.80, GoM $14.60, total $9.06. And now in Q2 2024, Permian $6.95, Eagle Ford $8.25, Bakken $9.65, GoM $13.20, total $7.98.

The Permian, which accounts for 65% of our 185,000 BOE/d production, has seen the sharpest decline—26% over five years—thanks to scale in the Delaware Basin. Eagle Ford improved 32% YoY, driven by gas-rich laterals amid Henry Hub prices holding above $2.50/MMBtu. Bakken's progress reflects reduced water handling costs post-flare minimization initiatives, while GoM's higher baseline reflects subsea tie-backs and hurricane preparedness, but even there, we've shaved 29% since 2019.

Inflation headwinds peaked in 2022 with tubular and proppant costs up 15-20%, but we've decoupled OpEx growth from the 8% industry-wide services inflation tracked by Novi Labs, holding our increases to just 2% in FY2023.

Our success stems from a multi-pronged strategy blending technology, supply chain optimization, and regional tailoring. Let me unpack the key initiatives.

First, drilling and completion efficiencies, accounting for 40% impact: We've adopted simultaneous operations on multi-well pads in the Permian, averaging 4-6 wells per pad versus the industry's 3-well norm. This dropped D&C costs per lateral foot by 18% YoY to $650/ft. Partnerships with Halliburton for our ApexFlow hydraulic fracturing fleet—using electrified pumps and recycled water—reduced fuel costs by 25% and emissions by 30%, aligning with ESG mandates from BlackRock-led investors.

Second, digital and automation initiatives, 25% impact: Rolled out AspenTech's HYSYS digital twins across 80% of Permian assets, enabling predictive maintenance that cut unplanned downtime 22% and workover spend $0.45/BOE. AI-driven reservoir modeling from SLB's Delfi platform optimized choke management in Eagle Ford, lifting runtimes to 92% and trimming artificial lift expenses—ESP failures down 35%.

Third, supply chain and hedging discipline, 20% impact: Locked in 70% of 2024 sand volumes at $22/ton via multi-year contracts with Hi-Crush, shielding us from the 10% spot price spike. Regional hedging on diesel and chemicals—60% covered at $2.40/gallon—offset 80% of inflation. In Bakken, we've localized water sourcing to 95% produced water, slashing trucking costs $1.20/BOE.

Fourth, asset optimization and rationalization, 15% impact: Divested high-cost, low-IP legacy Bakken wells, OpEx over $12/BOE, for $150 million, reallocating to Permian bolt-ons. In GoM, subsea pumping systems on our Thunder Horse field mimic Chevron's Anchor program, deferring $50 million in platform CapEx and dropping LOE $1.80/BOE.

Regionally, Permian's scale gives us leverage—negotiating 15% discounts on services versus independents. Eagle Ford benefits from NGL purity improvements via fractionation upgrades at our Cotulla plant, boosting netbacks $3/BOE. Bakken's focus on long laterals over 12,000 ft and GoM's minimal deferral strategy post-Hurricane Ida have been pivotal.

These efforts position us firmly in the lower cost quartile, with breakevens at $42/BOE half-cycle—resilient even if WTI dips to $65 on recession fears. Peers like Occidental and ConocoPhillips are chasing similar gains via M&A scale, but our $1.2 billion organic FCF in H1 reflects organic execution.

Looking ahead, we target $7.50/BOE by YE2025 through Phase 2 of our Efficiency 2.0 program: drone-based integrity inspections saving $0.30/BOE, and Permian cube development with 48-well pads. Risks include labor shortages—we're countering with 15% wage incentives—and potential frac crew day rates rising 5-7% per EIA forecasts.

I'll now turn to our adjusted EBITDA, which came in at $3.2 billion for the quarter, representing a robust 28% year-over-year increase from $2.5 billion in Q2 2023. On a full-year trailing twelve months basis, EBITDA reached $12.1 billion, up 22% YoY. This performance underscores the strength of our integrated portfolio and our disciplined execution amid a volatile macro environment. Let me break down the key drivers behind this outperformance.

First, realized pricing was a major tailwind. Our upstream realizations averaged $82 per barrel for Brent-equivalent crude, up 15% from $71 last year, driven by Brent crude averaging $85/bbl this quarter versus $75 in Q2 '23. Natural gas realizations held steady at $3.50 per Mcf in the US, benefiting from Henry Hub prices around $3.80, while our LNG cargoes from the Gulf Coast achieved premiums of $12/MMBtu over JKM. Downstream, however, refining cracks softened to $18/bbl from $25 last year due to seasonal demand weakness and higher Chinese product imports, partially offsetting upstream gains.

Production volumes grew 8% YoY to 1.45 million BOE/d, with upstream output up 12% to 1.2 million BOE/d. In the Permian Basin, where we hold 450,000 net acres, we brought online 45 new horizontal wells in the Delaware sub-basin, averaging 1,200 ft laterals with multi-stage fracs using our proprietary ceramic proppant blends. This drove a 25% YoY increase in Permian volumes to 650,000 BOE/d, with initial production rates exceeding 2,000 BOE/d per well—well ahead of our type curve. Efficiency gains here were notable: drilling times dropped 20% to 18 days per well, and frac stages per day improved 15% thanks to our automated walking rigs and real-time data analytics from our partnership with Halliburton’s DecisionSpace platform.

Bakken and Eagle Ford contributed another 7% volume growth, leveraging our infill drilling program targeting middle Bakken benches with 3-mile laterals. Internationally, North Sea production rose 5% to 120,000 BOE/d following the tie-back of our Fenja field satellite to the Norwegian Continental Shelf, though offset by planned turnarounds at our UK Brent field assets. In the Middle East, our 30% JV stake in the ADNOC-operated Ruwais offshore block maintained steady liftings at 80,000 bbl/d, with realizations boosted by OPEC+ quota stability.

On the cost side, we delivered $450 million in EBITDA uplift from operational efficiencies. Upstream lease operating expenses fell 10% to $8.50/BOE, driven by our Fit-for-Basin initiative, which optimized chemical usage in fracs by 18% via AI-driven reservoir modeling—similar to what we've seen peers like Pioneer Natural Resources achieve. DD&A held flat at $12/BOE despite higher volumes, reflecting our low-cost inventory. Midstream gathered volumes grew 10% with the commissioning of our Pecos River NGL pipeline expansion to 200,000 bbl/d capacity, generating $150 million in fee-based EBITDA and insulating us from Waha hub basis blows.

Strategic moves amplified these dynamics. Our Q1 divestiture of non-core Bakken vertical wells for $400 million reduced high-breakeven inventory, improving our portfolio FCF yield to 18%. Hedging covered 60% of Q3 oil volumes at $80/bbl floors, mitigating WTI-Brent spreads that widened to $4/bbl. Meanwhile, we progressed our CCUS pilots in the Permian, capturing 1 million tons CO2 YTD with our Denbury-acquired CO2 infrastructure, qualifying for 45Q tax credits worth $50 million annually at scale.

Challenges included upstream inflation, with tubular and sand costs up 12% YoY, though our frame agreements with NOV and Liberty Oilfield Services capped this at mid-single digits. Downstream margins compressed 25% due to 2-3-2-1 cracks averaging $16/bbl at our Gulf Coast refineries, exacerbated by PM2.5-compliant fuel oil specs ahead of IMO 2020 residuals.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 EBITDA of $3.0-3.4 billion, with Permian D&C capex focused on 50% oil-cut laterals and international growth via our Brazil pre-salt wildcat spuds. Our long-term strategy remains anchored in high-return shale, advantaged LNG exports, and low-carbon transitions, positioning us for sustained 15-20% annual EBITDA growth through the cycle.

Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. As we wrap up our Q2 results, I'd like to dive deeper into our capital allocation framework, which remains laser-focused on maximizing total shareholder return while positioning Apex Energy for long-term value creation in this dynamic Oil & Gas landscape. With WTI averaging $76 per barrel and Brent at $79 this quarter—buoyed by steady global demand and OPEC+ discipline—our upstream portfolio generated a robust $4.8 billion in free cash flow, up 15% year-over-year. This gives us ample dry powder to execute on our three core priorities: sustainable dividends, opportunistic share buybacks, and disciplined reinvestment. Let me break it down.

First, dividends: committing to shareholder-friendly payouts. Our dividend policy is the bedrock of our capital return strategy, designed for resilience across cycles. Today, we're announcing a 12% increase in our quarterly dividend to $0.55 per share, payable August 15th to shareholders of record by July 25th. This brings our annualized dividend to $2.20 per share, yielding approximately 3.8% at current prices—competitive with peers like ExxonMobil's 3.4% and Chevron's 4.1%, but with a lower payout ratio of just 38% of adjusted earnings.

This hike reflects our confidence in sustained free cash flow generation. Over the past 12 months, we've returned $3.2 billion in dividends, supported by a coverage ratio north of 1.8x even at $60 WTI sensitivity. We've maintained or grown the dividend through every downturn since 2014, including the 2020 trough when we slashed capex by 50% but preserved payouts via cost-out initiatives like automating rig fleets in the Permian. Looking ahead, we target a 40-45% payout of FCF in 2025, scaling with cash flow as LNG export demand from Asia—projected to rise 12% per Shell's LNG Outlook—bolsters our Gulf Coast positions.

Second, share buybacks: disciplined repurchases at attractive valuations. When our stock trades below intrinsic value, buybacks are our highest-return use of capital, often outyielding organic investments. We've repurchased $1.1 billion in shares year-to-date under our $5 billion authorization, retiring 4.2% of outstanding shares at an average price of $52—about 18% below our $65 NAV per share estimate from our internal DCF models incorporating 10% IRR hurdles.

This quarter alone, we bought back $450 million, focusing on open-market transactions and accelerated share repurchase agreements with counterparties like JPMorgan. Our framework is opportunistic yet framework-driven: we pause buybacks if EV/EBITDA exceeds 5.5x our peer median, currently at 4.8x versus Occidental's 5.2x, or if better growth opportunities emerge. Post-buyback, we've seen EPS accretion of 8% this year, enhancing ROCE from 14% to 16%. With $3.9 billion remaining authorized, we expect to deploy another $1.5-2 billion in 2025, contingent on valuations and macro conditions like potential Fed rate cuts supporting multiples expansion.

Third, reinvestment: high-return growth with a discipline filter. While returns to shareholders are paramount, we're not standing still on growth. Our $10.5 billion 2025 capex budget—flat to 2024—prioritizes projects with IRRs above 20% and paybacks under 2 years, allocating 55% to growth capex, $5.8 billion, and 45% to base maintenance, $4.7 billion. This yields projected production growth of 7% to 1.45 MMBOE/d, with all-in breakevens at $45 WTI.

Regionally, we're doubling down on Tier-1 assets: Permian Basin, 45% of capex, $4.8 billion: Drilling 450 wells across our 250,000 net acres in the Delaware and Midland sub-basins, targeting 20%+ oil cuts via extended laterals, 12,000 ft+, and simultaneous frac crews. We've deployed digital twin technology—partnering with Schlumberger's Delfi platform—to optimize completions, reducing cycle times by 25% and boosting well productivity 15% YoY. This supports 150,000 BOE/d growth, with hedges covering 70% of 2025 volumes at $68 strip.

Guyana Offshore, 20% of capex, $2.1 billion: Advancing our Yellowtail Phase 2 FPSO with SBM Offshore, sanctioning first oil in H2 2026 at 220,000 BOPD gross. Payback under 18 months at $70 Brent, with 25% working interest yielding 40,000 net BOE/d. Amid Exxon-led consortium momentum, this de-risks our Stabroek block portfolio.

Gulf of Mexico and North Sea, 15% of capex, $1.6 billion: High-margin tie-backs like our Winterfell deepwater project, online Q4 2024, and Johan Sverdrup extensions, leveraging subsea electrification to cut opex 20%. These assets boast 25%+ IRRs, insulated from shale volatility.

Emerging bets, 10% of capex, $1.1 billion: $500 million into CCUS hubs in the Permian, qualifying for 45Q tax credits and aligning with IRA incentives—targeting 5 MMTPA capture by 2028. Plus, LNG midstream stakes akin to Cheniere's Corpus Christi expansions, capitalizing on Europe's 20 Bcf/d import surge post-Ukraine.

The remaining 10% funds tech initiatives like AI-driven reservoir modeling with Halliburton's DecisionSpace and rig electrification pilots, slashing Scope 1 emissions 15% toward our 2030 net-zero ambitions for new developments.

In summary, our framework—80/20 split between returns, dividends plus buybacks at ~$7-8 billion, and reinvestment—delivers 12-15% TSR potential, outpacing the XLE index's 10% historical average. We've returned $12 billion to shareholders since 2022 while growing production 25%, proving our model's resilience. Risks like Red Sea disruptions or China demand softness are hedged 60% through 2025, with $8 billion liquidity and a 1.1x net debt/EBITDA providing buffer.

We're not chasing volume for volume's sake like some independents; it's about capital velocity in a $80-90 oil world.

I will now turn the call over to Maria for an operational update.

Maria Gonzalez: Thank you, David. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 185,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought several new pads online in the Permian, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives, including enhanced water recycling and automation across our key basins.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Chris Baker with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Chris Baker: Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the operating expenses per BOE trends and your cost management strategies going forward?

Sarah Thompson: Good morning, Chris. David covered this extensively, but to recap and add a bit more color, our OpEx per BOE hit a record low of $7.98 this quarter, down 12% YoY, driven by basin-specific efficiencies like SIMOPS in the Permian and digital twins reducing downtime. We're targeting $7.50 by year-end 2025 with Efficiency 2.0, including drone inspections and larger cube developments. This keeps us in the lowest cost quartile, resilient to downside oil prices.

Operator: Our next question comes from Elena Vasquez with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Elena Vasquez: Good morning. What are your expectations for capital allocation priorities, especially dividends and buybacks?

David Patel: Good morning, Elena. Our framework prioritizes returns: we just raised the quarterly dividend 12% to $0.55, targeting 40-45% FCF payout. Buybacks are opportunistic; we've done $1.1 billion YTD at attractive prices, with $3.9 billion left. Reinvestment stays disciplined at high-IRR projects only, balancing 80% returns to 20% growth for optimal TSR.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Reilly with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Reilly: Could you please provide more color on future development plans and resource potential?

Maria Gonzalez: Good morning, Tom. Sarah laid out our 5-year plan well: ramping to 400,000 Boe/d by 2027 via Permian extensions, Eagle Ford Pearsall, Haynesville HyperFrac, GoM Winterfell, and Guyana upside. With 3.4 billion Boe 3P reserves and strong replacement ratios, we have over 30 years R/P at 3P, all funded from FCF with hedges in place.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to Sarah Thompson for closing remarks.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator. In summary, we are pleased with our performance in Q2 2024. We remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering value to our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
